security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives caused by Markdown code fences, inline backtick references, and Kubernetes policy terms. One network template still allows broad HTTPS egress to 0.0.0.0/0, and two RBAC examples show overly broad access patterns that should be narrowed before publication. No prompt injection text was found in the reviewed files.

remediation.suggestion: Replace 0.0.0.0/0 with approved destination CIDRs or clearly mark the template as a temporary placeholder that must be narrowed.
Use a namespaced Role with resourceNames for specific secrets and avoid list or watch permissions on secrets.
Replace wildcard resources and verbs with explicit resources and required actions for the target workflow.

static_findings.snippet: - If detailed examples are required, open `resources/implementation-playbook.md`.
- Set up RBAC for least-privilege access

semantic_findings.title: Overbroad Cluster-Wide Secret Access Example
semantic_findings.description: SKILL.md presents a ClusterRole named secret-reader with get, watch, and list access to all secrets. If copied into production, this can expose credentials across the cluster.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The RBAC example directly grants cluster-wide read, watch, and list permissions on secrets. The risk is clear because Kubernetes secrets often contain credentials.

semantic_findings.title: Wildcard Namespace Admin RBAC Example
semantic_findings.description: references/rbac-patterns.md includes a namespace-admin Role that grants wildcard resources and wildcard verbs in production. This pattern can allow excessive control over namespace resources.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The example explicitly uses wildcard resources and verbs. Later guidance warns against wildcards, but the unsafe sample remains easy to copy.

content.value_statement: Kubernetes policy work is easy to make too broad or inconsistent. This skill guides network policies, RBAC, pod security, and admission controls for safer clusters.
actual_capabilities: Guides default-deny NetworkPolicy design and namespace isolation.
Provides RBAC role and binding patterns for service accounts and users.
Explains Pod Security Standards labels for privileged, baseline, and restricted modes.
Shows pod security context settings for non-root execution and dropped capabilities.
Covers OPA Gatekeeper and Istio security policy examples.
Includes kubectl troubleshooting checks for NetworkPolicy and RBAC issues.
limitations: Does not validate manifests against a live Kubernetes cluster.
Examples require adaptation to each namespace, CNI, and application topology.
Does not replace a full threat model or compliance assessment.
Some templates include broad examples that must be narrowed before production use.

use_cases.title: Build namespace isolation
use_cases.description: Create default-deny policies and explicit service-to-service access for production namespaces.

use_cases.title: Review application permissions
use_cases.description: Check service account roles, bindings, and secret access before an application release.

use_cases.title: Prepare compliance controls
use_cases.description: Map Kubernetes security controls to CIS and NIST expectations for audit planning.

prompt_templates.title: Create a starter policy
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a default-deny NetworkPolicy plan for namespace <namespace>. Include required DNS access and explain what traffic remains blocked.

prompt_templates.title: Harden a workload
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this Kubernetes workload for pod security issues. Recommend Pod Security Standards labels and container securityContext changes.

prompt_templates.title: Review RBAC access
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these Role, ClusterRole, and Binding manifests. Identify excessive permissions and propose least-privilege replacements.

prompt_templates.title: Design multi-tenant controls
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a security policy model for a multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster. Include network isolation, RBAC, admission control, and verification steps.

output_examples.input: I need to isolate frontend, API, and database pods in production.
output: Start with a default-deny policy for ingress and egress.
Allow frontend traffic only to the API service port.
Allow API traffic only to the database port and DNS.
Keep database pods unreachable from other application tiers.

output_examples.input: Review this service account for secret access.
output: Use a namespaced Role for the required secret only.
Prefer get on a named secret instead of list or watch.
Bind the Role only to the application service account.

output_examples.input: Prepare compliance notes for Kubernetes policy controls.
output_examples.output: The result groups controls for network segmentation, least-privilege access, pod hardening, admission control, and audit logging.

best_practices: Start with default-deny network policies and add explicit allowed flows.
Use least-privilege RBAC with named resources when possible.
Validate policy behavior in a staging cluster before production rollout.
anti_patterns: Do not copy broad egress policies into production without narrowing destinations.
Do not grant wildcard RBAC verbs or resources for routine workloads.
Do not give applications broad list or watch access to Kubernetes secrets.

faq.question: Does this skill create production-ready manifests automatically?
faq.answer: It provides policy guidance and examples. You must adapt and test manifests for your cluster and workloads.

faq.question: Can it validate NetworkPolicy behavior in my cluster?
faq.answer: No. It can suggest kubectl checks, but live validation requires access to your Kubernetes environment.

faq.question: Does it cover PodSecurityPolicy?
faq.answer: It focuses on Pod Security Standards because PodSecurityPolicy is removed from current Kubernetes releases.

faq.question: Can it help with RBAC least privilege?
faq.answer: Yes. It can review roles and bindings, then suggest narrower resources, verbs, and subjects.

faq.question: Does it support OPA Gatekeeper?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes examples for Gatekeeper constraint templates and constraints.

faq.question: Is it useful for compliance work?
faq.answer: Yes. It can organize Kubernetes security controls for CIS and NIST planning, but it is not an audit certification tool.
